narrative:
The model estimated an 81% probability that you will leave your job, which is high enough that the organization treated retention risk as the main reason to deny the promotion. This is not a finding about your worth or performance; it means the pattern of your situation looks much more like employees who exit than like those who stay.

The strongest reason was that you have other job opportunities. Among employees predicted to stay, only about one in four had other opportunities, while you do, and this was the top influence pushing the prediction toward leaving. Your overall experience of 6–10 years was the second strongest factor; it is common, but still less common among stayers than 1–5 years, and it added another push toward leaving. Your monthly salary of 11k–15k SAR was the third factor. That band is higher than most employees predicted to stay—only about 13% are in it and most earn less—but in your profile it still contributed a smaller push toward leaving rather than toward staying. All three leading signals pointed in the same direction.

Before revisiting promotion, the organization should discuss whether you are actively considering external roles and what career path, promotion criteria, recognition, and support would make staying worthwhile. You should use that conversation to clarify your goals and ask for a concrete development plan. Treat the high leaving probability as an early warning: retention action now is more useful than waiting until you have already decided to go.
